summary: Govind Sakharam Kathavate was an Indologist who succeeded Ramkrishna Gopal Bhandarkar to the Sanskrit chair at Deccan College Post-Graduate and Research Institute.

Govind Swamirao Gai (1917–1995) worked in Indology, archaeology, and linguistics. Succeeding Dineschandra Sircar, he served as Government Epigraphist for India and Chief Epigraphist for India at the Archaeological Survey of India, and later as epigraphy consultant for the AIIS.

Govindlal Hargovind Bhatt was an Indologist who taught Arunoday Natvarlal Jani. He served as a professor at Baroda College (attested 1933–1939) and later as director of the Oriental Institute, Vadodara (attested 1953–1957).

Grace S. Fong (born 1948) is a Sinologist who studied at the University of British Columbia and McGill University. She was a professor at Smith College (~1984–1986) and later associate professor and department chair at McGill University (~1992).

Graeme MacQueen (1948–2023) was a scholar of Buddhist and religious studies who earned his doctorate at Harvard University under Masatoshi Nagatomi. He served as a lecturer at McMaster University (~1989–2013).
Graham E. Clarke (died 1998) was a Tibetologist who held positions at the Institute of Development Studies and as a senior member at the University of Oxford (attested 1998).
Graham Lock is a scholar in Buddhist studies and linguistics who studied under teachers Hsuan Hua and Saddhaloka Bhikkhu.

Graham Priest (born 1948) studied at Cambridge and LSE. Working in philosophy and Buddhist studies, he held positions at Melbourne, CUNY, and St Andrews, along with a 1990 visiting fellowship at Clare Hall, Cambridge.

Graves Champney Haughton (1788–1849) studied at East India Company College before succeeding Alexander Hamilton as Professor of Hindú Literature and the History of Asia there (~1817–1827). He also served as secretary of the Royal Asiatic Society (~1831–1832).

Gray Tuttle is a Tibetologist and historian who earned his Ph.D. at Harvard in 2002 under Leonard van der Kuijp, Philip A. Kuhn, and William C. Kirby. He later served as associate professor at Columbia University (attested 2008–2015).
Graziadio Isaia Ascoli (1829–1907) was a linguist and Indologist who founded the Archivio Glottologico Italiano and became a professor at the Accademia Scientifico-Letteraria di Milano in 1860.

Greg Bailey is an Indologist who studied under Madeleine Biardeau and completed his doctorate under J. Durham. He held academic posts at La Trobe University, where he was attested as a professor in 2004.
Gregor Ahn (born 1958) is a scholar of religious and Iranian/Central Asian studies who studied under Hans-Joachim Klimkeit (~1980–1991). He held a post at Heidelberg University around 2002.

Gregory Forgues is a scholar of Tibetology and Buddhist studies who earned a Magister der Philosophie at the University of Vienna, supervised by Helmut Tauscher and Birgit Kellner, alongside traditional teachers including Dzongsar Jamyang Khyentse Rinpoche and Namkhai Norbu.

Gregory Max Seton is a scholar of Buddhist studies, Tibetology, and Indology. He earned degrees from Naropa University, UC Santa Barbara, and a D.Phil from Wolfson College, Oxford (2015), studying under Vesna A. Wallace and Alexis Sanderson.

Gregory P. A. Levine (born 1963) studied at Oberlin College and Princeton University. He works in Japanology, Buddhist studies, and art history, serving as an associate professor of the history of art at UC Berkeley (~2002).

Gregory Schopen (born 1947), an Indologist and Buddhist studies scholar, earned his PhD at the Australian National University under J.W. de Jong and Tissa Rajapatirana. He held professorships at Indiana, UT Austin, and UCLA, alongside posts at Brown and Stanford.

Grigorij Maksimovič Bongard-Levin (1933–2008) studied at the MSU Institute of Asian and African Studies under George Roerich. He held long-term posts at the Institute of Oriental Studies, Moscow State University, and the Institute of World History.

Guang Xing (born 1962) completed his PhD at SOAS under Tadeusz Skorupski and Timothy H. Barrett. Specializing in Buddhist studies, he became an assistant professor at the University of Hong Kong (~2003) and held visiting professorships at UBC.

Guangchang Fang (born 1948) is a scholar in Buddhist studies and Sinology who served as a researcher at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences (~1986–2000) and as a professor at Shanghai Normal University (~2004).
